definition: Voice and data links between an aircraft and the ground that pass through a satellite. Used over oceans, deserts and the poles, where radar and VHF radio do not reach.
A circular orbit 35,786 km above the equator. A satellite there goes round once per turn of the Earth, so from the ground it seems to stay in one spot in the sky.
An orbit a few hundred to about 2,000 km up. Satellites there circle the Earth in about 100 minutes, so each one crosses the sky in a few minutes and many are needed to cover the globe.

The area on the Earth from which a satellite is high enough in the sky to be used. A GEO footprint covers almost half the Earth; a LEO footprint is a few thousand kilometres across and moves with the satellite.
How high a satellite appears above the horizon, in degrees: 0° is on the horizon, 90° is straight overhead. Links need a satellite a few degrees above the horizon.
Switching a link from one satellite to another, for example when a low-orbit satellite is about to set below the horizon and the next one is rising. It can cause a brief interruption.
A radio link directly between two satellites. Low-orbit constellations such as Iridium use them to pass a message around the world until a satellite can send it down to a ground gateway.
The large dish on the ground that connects a satellite to terrestrial networks, and from there to air traffic control. For low-orbit systems it is usually called a gateway.
The delay between sending a message and it arriving. For a satellite link it includes the trip through space (distance divided by the speed of light) plus time spent in equipment and queues.
Radio frequencies of roughly 12 to 18 GHz. Used for high-speed passenger internet via satellite. Heavy rain weakens it much more than L-band.
Radio frequencies of roughly 26 to 40 GHz (in satellite use, often 20 GHz down and 30 GHz up). Carries a lot of data but fades strongly in heavy rain.
Weakening of a radio signal as it passes through rain, because the drops absorb and scatter it. It grows quickly with frequency: tiny at L-band, large at Ku and Ka band.
Voice calls between pilots and air traffic control made through a satellite system instead of HF or VHF radio.
ADS-B receivers carried on low-orbit satellites. They pick up the position broadcasts aircraft already send and relay them to the ground, so controllers can see aircraft over oceans and poles.
A satellite operator whose geostationary satellites provide aeronautical safety voice and data services, such as Classic Aero and SwiftBroadband Safety.
A constellation of 66 active low-orbit satellites in six near-polar planes, linked to each other in space. It covers the whole Earth, including the poles.
One turn of the Earth measured against the distant stars: 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds, a little shorter than the 24-hour solar day.
